items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: Oh, yeah, well he was contractor, you know, Jimmy Jones. We could really read music... That was on a date with Barry Galbraith on guitar, Art Farmer on trumpet, Cannonball Adderley on saxophone, and yours truly on bass.

ctx.x: It was beautiful to see the expression on your face and Osie’s and Hank, when the new music was put in front of you. I mean like, “Ayyy, yeah, hey look what we got,” you know. Wow, like it was like somebody bought you a new gift. Cause Jimmy Jones was writing then, and—

Oh, yeah, well he was contractor, you know, Jimmy Jones. We could really read music and that was the thing that I thank my mother this very day for that, because I wanted to play everything, and she says, “You got to learn to read that music.” And that’s what we could do, we could read. And young Adderley’s on the boat here, and yesterday on the Meet the Stars he was telling some people about a picture I have, I have a picture I took of Cannonball, sitting down with a stack of music and it’s falling down off the…
Well he was the — Julian was articulate in more ways than one.

items.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jimmy Jones wrote a piece for Sarah Vaughn using Richard Davis and yours truly on it.

ctx.x: When did you do that or how did you do… how did that come about.

Well we kept dreaming about it. Pops Foster‟s really dreaming like I mentioned. He always wanted t do it. Pops Foster died. We had this… we still have a mutual admiration society among bass players. We are really pretty close because we come one to a customer in jazz, only one bass player. It‟s like your momma is your momma. If you‟ve got a brother, that‟s still your mom. You know, that‟s your mom. It‟s his mom too but that‟s your mom. Well that‟s the way bass players feel. I‟m the best bass player in the band…

items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: I had some of the best string players out of New York. I had Dick Hyman and Hank Jones on piano. Ossie Johnson and Milt Hinton, you know.

ctx.x: Because Milt Hinton sent me a thick thing, you know, and every time he would mark it in the red -- I was reading through it and he would put a red pencil note and say, 'This is your teacher.' Well, Dr. Anderson, you know? Oh, he taught me counterpoint, and oh, he's a massive musician. And I don't know whether he's still there or not, but he's been there for years. He went from Kentucky State to I think it was either Oberlin or Antioch, in Ohio, you know?

items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: I don't know if Milt even knows this was stated by Nance, because I haven't talked to Milt lately.

ctx.x: But he mentioned in that book, he says he couldn't move to the first chair because the guy that really held the first chair down was the -- became a very famous bass player, Milton Hinton. And that was a -- I don't know if Milt even knows this was stated by Nance, because I haven't talked to Milt lately.
